title: Notes from E-Marking Centre on SSC-I Chemistry Annual Examinations 2025
subject: Chemistry
introduction: This document has been produced for the teachers and candidates of Secondary School Certificate (SSC) Part I Chemistry. It contains comments on candidates’ responses to the 2025 SSC-I Examination indicating the quality of the responses and highlighting their relative strengths and weaknesses.
generalObservations: Candidates generally demonstrated a satisfactory understanding of core chemistry concepts, particularly in areas such as chemical bonding, writing correct chemical equations for different reactions, separation techniques, and recognising the structural features of voltaic cells. Better responses reflected clarity in scientific reasoning, appropriate use of terminology, and structured explanations aligned with the question requirements. However, a significant proportion of weaker responses revealed persistent misconceptions, surface-level understanding, and difficulty applying concepts across different contexts.

questions.questionText:
The atom of an element X has 8 neutrons, 8 protons and 8 electrons.
a. Identify element X.
b. If the element X forms an ion X^-2, then how many valence electrons will this ion contain?
c. An isotope of this element X has mass number 18. How many neutrons are there in an atom of this isotope?
questions.sloText: Calculate the mass (nucleon) number, number of electrons, protons and neutrons of atoms and ions;
checkingHints: 1 mark for the correct identification of element X (Oxygen)
1 mark for the correct number of valence electrons in X^-2 (8 valence electrons)
1 mark for the correct number of neutrons in the given isotope (10 neutrons)
questions.overallPerformance: Overall, candidates showed good performance on this question. A considerable number demonstrated commendable analytical thinking by correctly identifying the element using the atomic number, applying the octet rule, and accurately calculating the number of neutrons in an isotope.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses correctly identified element X as oxygen by linking the atomic number (8 protons) to its position in the periodic table. They recognized that gaining two electrons completes its octet (8 valence electrons). In part (c), they accurately applied the formula: neutrons = mass number (18) - atomic number (8) = 10.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses confused electron gain with valence electron count, stating that X^2- has only 2 valence electrons, or subtracted electrons assuming -2 meant losing electrons. Several candidates gave the mass number 18 as the neutron count rather than subtracting atomic number.
suggestions: Use concept-building worksheets focusing on atomic number, elemental identity, electronic configuration, and ion formation.
Reinforce the distinction between total electrons and valence electrons.
Emphasize that gaining electrons completes the octet (8 valence electrons) in non-metal anions.
questions.modelAnswer:
a. Oxygen (O)
b. 8 valence electrons
c. 10 neutrons (18 - 8 = 10)

questions.questionText:
a. Define the term, ‘electron affinity’.
b. Describe, with a reason, the trend of electron affinity within a group of the periodic table.
questions.sloText: Explain the periodic trend of the following within a group and a period of the periodic table: a. shielding effect b. electronegativity c. atomic radii d. electron affinity e. ionisation energy.
checkingHints: 1 mark for the definition of electron affinity
1 mark for the electron affinity trend in a group (decreases down the group)
1 mark for writing the reason for the trend in the group
questions.overallPerformance: Overall, candidates' responses reflected a mixed understanding of electron affinity. While some correctly defined the term and explained the group trend using atomic size and shielding effects, many confused it with related concepts such as electronegativity or ionisation energy.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses accurately defined electron affinity as the amount of energy released when a neutral atom in the gaseous state gains an electron to form a negative ion. In part (b), they correctly stated that electron affinity decreases down a group due to increasing atomic radius and enhanced shielding.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses mistakenly defined electron affinity as electronegativity or ionisation energy. In part (b), they claimed electron affinity increases down the group or linked it to electron count without considering atomic radius and shielding.
suggestions: Strengthen conceptual clarity by comparing periodic properties using visual organizers like Venn diagrams.
Use conceptual animations demonstrating energy release during electron gain.
Practice question interpretation distinguishing between electron affinity, electronegativity, and ionisation energy.
questions.modelAnswer:
a. Electron affinity is the amount of energy released when an electron is added to the outermost shell of an isolated neutral gaseous atom to form an anion.
b. Electron affinity decreases down a group because atomic radius and shielding effect increase, weakening nuclear attraction for an added electron.

questions.questionText:
a. Which has a higher boiling point, oxygen gas or liquid water?
b. Give reasons with reference to both oxygen gas and liquid water to support your answer to part a.
questions.sloText: Explain the properties of liquids and the factors that affect them: a. evaporation b. vapour pressure c. boiling point d. freezing point e. diffusion f. density g. compressibility;
checkingHints: 1 mark for the correct identification (liquid water)
1 mark for writing the correct reason for liquid water (strong hydrogen bonding)
1 mark for writing the correct reason for oxygen gas (weak London dispersion forces)
questions.overallPerformance: Overall, candidates’ performance on this question was generally strong, with a substantial proportion achieving full marks by correctly identifying liquid water and referencing hydrogen bonding.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses contrasted the strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding in water (which requires substantial energy to overcome) with the very weak van der Waals (London dispersion) forces holding non-polar O2 molecules.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses incorrectly attributed boiling point differences to molar mass, particle size, or density rather than intermolecular forces.
suggestions: Incorporate visual aids and short videos clearly depicting hydrogen bonding vs van der Waals interactions.
Conduct comparative case studies of boiling points across H2O, O2, CH4, and NH3.
questions.modelAnswer:
a. Liquid water has a higher boiling point.
b. Liquid water has strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding requiring high energy to break, whereas non-polar oxygen gas has only weak London dispersion forces.

questions.questionText:
Explain why the
a. first ionisation energy decreases down the group of alkali metals.
b. second ionisation energy of sodium is higher than that of magnesium.
questions.sloText: Differentiate between ionisation energies of alkali and alkaline earth metals;
checkingHints: 1 mark for writing the cause (atomic size increases / shielding effect increases)
1 mark for writing its effect (nuclear attraction on outer electron decreases)
1 mark for writing correct reason about high 2nd IE of sodium (removal from stable noble gas octet)
1 mark for writing correct reason about low 2nd IE of magnesium (removal from outer 3s sub-shell)
questions.overallPerformance: Overall, candidates' performance on this question was unsatisfactory, with only a small proportion achieving full marks due to incomplete cause-and-effect explanations.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses clearly explained that down the group, atomic size and shielding increase, weakening effective nuclear attraction. In part (b), they linked sodium's high second IE to breaking a stable inner noble-gas octet (2p6), whereas magnesium's second electron is removed from the outer 3s shell.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses failed to connect atomic radius to weakened nuclear pull. In part (b), many did not refer to electronic configurations or confused nuclear charge with effective nuclear charge.
suggestions: Use guided cause-and-effect response frames: 'As atomic radius increases... this causes nuclear pull to... therefore energy required is...'
Practice writing electronic configurations of Na+ and Mg+ to visualize electron removal from inner vs valence shells.
questions.modelAnswer:
a. First IE decreases down alkali metals because atomic radius and shielding increase, reducing nuclear attraction on the outer electron.
b. Sodium's second IE is higher because the second electron must be removed from a completely filled, stable noble-gas inner shell (2p6), whereas magnesium's second electron is removed from the outer valence 3s sub-shell.

questions.questionText:
In each of the given cases, provide a balanced chemical equation and describe any TWO characteristics of a chemical reaction that occurs between:
i. Zinc granules and dilute sulphuric acid
ii. Calcium oxide (quicklime) and water
questions.sloText: Describe the formation and characteristics of chemical equations;
checkingHints: 1 mark for balanced equation for case i (Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2)
1 mark for describing each characteristic of case i (2 required)
1 mark for balanced equation for case ii (CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2)
1 mark for describing each characteristic of case ii (2 required)
questions.overallPerformance: Only a few candidates attempted this part, and overall performance was notably weak. Many faced difficulties with chemical formulas and linking reactions with observable characteristics.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses provided accurate equations: Zn(s) + H2SO4(aq) -> ZnSO4(aq) + H2(g) and CaO(s) + H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2(aq). They correctly identified gas evolution (effervescence of H2) and exothermic temperature rise.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses wrote incorrect formulas like Ca(OH)2 instead of CaO, or zinc sulphide instead of zinc sulphate, and provided vague descriptions unrelated to chemical evidence.
suggestions: Conduct laboratory demonstrations showing gas bubbling and temperature rise.
Practice writing and balancing chemical equations from word descriptions.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2 (Characteristics: effervescence of hydrogen gas; exothermic reaction).
ii. CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 (Characteristics: vigorous heat liberation; formation of alkaline slaked lime solution).

questions.questionText:
You have a solution of copper(II) sulphate in water. You want to obtain pure, solid copper(II) sulphate from it.
i. Describe why the technique of filtering copper(II) sulphate solution will not work.
ii. Which method will you use instead? Give a reason to support your answer.
iii. Describe how you will obtain pure, solid copper(II) sulphate in THREE steps using the method identified in part ii.
checkingHints: 1 mark for describing why filtering does not work (CuSO4 is completely dissolved as ions in a true solution)
1 mark for naming crystallisation
1 mark for stating the correct reason for crystallisation
1 mark for writing each step of crystallisation (3 required)
questions.overallPerformance: This part was attempted by many candidates, with performance generally ranging from moderate to high. Most understood the principle of crystallisation, though procedural depth varied.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses explained that CuSO4 forms a true homogeneous solution where dissolved ions pass through filter pores. They named crystallisation and gave a clear 3-step sequence: 1. gentle heating to saturation, 2. slow cooling to grow crystals, 3. filtering and drying crystals between filter papers.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses failed to recognize that solutions have no solid residue and suggested electroplating or reduction instead of crystallisation, or skipped the critical cooling step.
suggestions: Use sequencing assessments where students arrange jumbled separation steps in correct logical order.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Filtration fails because CuSO4 is completely dissolved as solvated ions in a true solution; filter paper only separates insoluble particles.
ii. Crystallisation, because it recovers pure solid solute crystals from solution by evaporation and cooling without decomposition.
iii. Step 1: Gently heat solution to saturation. Step 2: Cool slowly at room temperature to allow crystals to grow. Step 3: Filter off crystals and dry between filter papers.

questions.questionText:
Given below are the dot and cross structures of ammonia and hydrogen chloride. These two molecules on combining form ammonium chloride.
i. Name the bond that joins nitrogen of ammonia and hydrogen of hydrogen chloride.
ii. Describe the formation of ammonium chloride.
iii. Write THREE differences between the bond identified in part i and the one that already exists between nitrogen and hydrogen in ammonia.
questions.sloText: Compare the formation and characteristics of coordinate covalent compounds with covalent compounds;
checkingHints: 1 mark for naming coordinate covalent bond
1 mark for describing donation of lone pair from nitrogen to H+ forming ammonium ion
1 mark for describing ionic bond between ammonium ion and chloride ion
1 mark for each difference between coordinate covalent and covalent bonds (3 required)
questions.overallPerformance: Performance was low to moderate. While some understood coordinate covalent bonding, many omitted the second ionic stage or confused bond differences with physical properties of compounds.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses named coordinate covalent bond (dative bond). They described two distinct stages: lone pair donation from N to H+ forming NH4+, followed by electrostatic ionic attraction with Cl-. In part (iii), they distinguished origin of shared electrons (one atom vs both), donor/acceptor roles, and arrow vs single line representation.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses failed to recognize coordinate covalent bonding, confusing it with simple covalent or hydrogen bonds, and failed to mention the ionic bond with chloride.
suggestions: Anchor bonding concepts using familiar examples: NH3 (covalent), NH4+ (coordinate covalent), and NH4Cl (ionic).
Practice drawing dot-and-cross diagrams highlighting lone pair donation.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Coordinate covalent bond (dative bond).
ii. Nitrogen of ammonia donates its lone pair to H+ from HCl forming NH4+; the NH4+ and Cl- ions then form an ionic bond.
iii. 1. Coordinate bond electrons come from one atom (N lone pair); covalent bond electrons are contributed equally by both atoms. 2. Coordinate bond has donor and acceptor; covalent bond involves mutual sharing. 3. Coordinate bond is shown by an arrow (->); covalent bond by a single line (-).

questions.questionText: Describe any SIX features of a voltaic cell (Galvanic cell).
questions.sloText: Differentiate between electrolytic and voltaic (Galvanic) cells;
checkingHints: 1 mark for writing each feature of a voltaic cell (any 6 required)
questions.overallPerformance: Performance was generally strong. Most candidates secured high marks by identifying valid structural and functional features of a voltaic cell.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses clearly described: 1. spontaneous chemical reaction producing electricity, 2. two half-cells with electrodes in electrolytes, 3. electron flow from anode to cathode, 4. salt bridge maintaining electrical neutrality, 5. oxidation at anode and reduction at cathode, 6. conversion of chemical energy to electrical energy.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses listed specific device applications ('used in batteries') or described a specific cell like Daniell cell rather than generic features.
suggestions: Demonstrate simple zinc-copper Daniell cells in the laboratory.
Use diagram-labelling exercises identifying anode, cathode, electron flow, and salt bridge.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Converts chemical energy into electrical energy.
2. Driven by a spontaneous redox reaction.
3. Composed of two separate half-cells connected by a wire and salt bridge.
4. Oxidation occurs at the negative anode.
5. Reduction occurs at the positive cathode.
6. Salt bridge allows ion migration to maintain electrical neutrality.
